subject: maths
title: Column Addition and Subtraction
seo_title: Year 5 Column Addition and Subtraction Worksheets: Large Numbers, Mental Methods and Multi-Step Problems
standard_text: Add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction); add and subtract numbers mentally with increasingly large numbers; use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy; solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why.
meta_desc: Free Year 5 maths worksheets on column addition and subtraction with 5- and 6-digit numbers, following the National Curriculum: exchanging across zeros, mental methods, rounding to check and multi-step word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Line up the ones, start on the right, and round to check.
key_sub: Big numbers work just like small ones: exchange when a column makes 10 or more, or when the top digit is smaller. Every 0 you pass becomes 9. Use a mental method when the numbers are round.
body_html:
The idea: line up the columns

Column addition and subtraction work the same way for big numbers. Write the numbers so ones are under ones, tens under tens, and so on up to the hundred thousands. Always start with the ones on the right.

When a column adds up to 10 or more, write the ones digit and exchange 10 for 1 in the next column on the left. Write the exchanged 1 small, under the answer line.

Column subtraction with exchanging

Always take the bottom digit from the top digit. If the top digit is smaller, exchange: take 1 from the next column on the left and make 10 more in this column. Cross out the old digit and write the new one above it.

Exchanging across zeros

If the next column is 0, there is nothing to take. Move left to the first digit that is not 0 and exchange from there. Every 0 you pass becomes 9.

Mental methods with large numbers

You do not always need columns. Look at the numbers first and choose a quick method.

CalculationQuick method
45,000 + 7,000Think in thousands: 45 + 7 = 52, so 52,000
230,000 − 90,000Think in ten thousands: 23 − 9 = 14, so 140,000
348,215 + 30,000Only the ten thousands change: 34 + 3 = 37, so 378,215
56,789 + 9,999Add 10,000, then take away 1: 66,788
84,312 − 19,998Take away 20,000, then add 2 back: 64,314
100,000 − 36,000Number bonds: 36,000 + 64,000 = 100,000

Round to check

Round each number and do the easier calculation. For 5-digit numbers, round to the nearest thousand. For 6-digit numbers, round to the nearest ten thousand.

Is it sensible?

Ruby says 61,248 − 29,875 = 41,373. Is she right?

Estimate: 61,000 − 30,000 = 31,000. Her answer is about 10,000 too big, so it is wrong. She did not change the 6 to 5 after exchanging. The correct answer is 31,373.

Answer: No, it should be 31,373

Use the inverse for an exact check: 31,373 + 29,875 = 61,248, which is the number you started with.

When a problem asks for an answer to the nearest thousand (or hundred), work out the exact answer first, then round it. Rounding every number before you calculate can give the wrong answer.

Multi-step problems

Read the question and ask: what do I need to find first? Decide whether each step is adding (putting together, more) or subtracting (taking away, how many left, how many more). Use columns for hard steps and mental methods for easy ones.

Two steps

A charity wants to raise £50,000. A fun run raised £18,465 and an online appeal raised £23,890. How much more does it need?

Step 1, money raised: £18,465 + £23,890 = £42,355. Step 2, money still needed: £50,000 − £42,355 = £7,645. Check: £7,645 + £42,355 = £50,000.

Answer: £7,645

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Forgetting the exchanged 1s (47,586 + 38,749 = 75,225)Write each exchanged 1 under the next column and add it in
Taking the smaller digit from the bigger one (61,248 − 29,875 = 48,633)Always take the bottom digit from the top digit. Exchange when the top is smaller
Not exchanging across the zeros (300,000 − 47,586 = 247,584)Go left to the first digit that is not 0. Each 0 you pass becomes 9
Lining up the numbers on the left (47,586 + 3,874 = 86,326)Line up the ones on the right
Rounding to the wrong place when checkingRound 5-digit numbers to the nearest thousand and 6-digit numbers to the nearest ten thousand

faq.q: What addition and subtraction do children learn in Year 5?
faq.a: Year 5 pupils add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits using column methods, and do mental calculations with large numbers. They also round to check answers and solve multi-step word problems.

faq.q: How do you teach column subtraction with zeros, like 300,000 − 47,586?
faq.a: Go left to the first digit that is not 0 and exchange from there: 300,000 becomes 2 hundred thousands, 9 in each zero column and 10 ones. Then subtract column by column to get 252,414.

faq.q: How can children check a big addition or subtraction answer?
faq.a: Round each number to estimate, for example 61,000 − 30,000 = 31,000 for 61,248 − 29,875. For an exact check, use the inverse: 31,373 + 29,875 = 61,248.

faq.q: When should Year 5 pupils use a mental method instead of columns?
faq.a: Use a mental method when the numbers are round or close to round, such as 230,000 − 90,000 or 56,789 + 9,999. Use columns when there are many exchanges.

items.e: 712,450 rounds to 710,000 and 368,900 rounds to 370,000. 710,000 − 370,000 = 340,000. The exact answer is 343,550, which is close to 340,000.

items.q: Amelia worked out 72,315 − 38,742 = 43,573. Round each number to the nearest thousand to estimate. Is her answer sensible?
items.e: Estimate: 72,000 − 39,000 = 33,000. Amelia's answer, 43,573, is about 10,000 bigger than the estimate. She exchanged 1 ten thousand for 10 thousands but did not change the 7 to 6. The correct answer is 33,573.

items.q: A charity raised £48,520 at a fun run and £27,640 online. A poster gives the total to the nearest thousand pounds. What does the poster say?
items.e: Work out the exact total first: £48,520 + £27,640 = £76,160. Then round to the nearest thousand: £76,000. Rounding each amount first gives £49,000 + £28,000 = £77,000, which is too far out.

items.q: A football club sold 34,862 tickets for one match and 29,418 tickets for the next. A report gives the difference to the nearest hundred. What does it say?
items.e: Work out the exact difference first: 34,862 − 29,418 = 5,444. Then round to the nearest hundred: 5,400. Rounding each number first gives 34,900 − 29,400 = 5,500, which is not accurate.

items.q: A town had 186,450 people. Then 12,780 people moved in and 4,935 people moved out. The council gives the new population to the nearest ten thousand. What does it say?
items.e: Work out the exact number first: 186,450 + 12,780 = 199,230, then 199,230 − 4,935 = 194,295. Round to the nearest ten thousand: 190,000. Rounding each number first gives 190,000 + 10,000 − 0 = 200,000, which is wrong.

items.q: Which calculation checks 524,316 − 287,452 = 236,864?
items.e: Addition is the inverse of subtraction. Add the answer to the number you took away: 236,864 + 287,452 = 524,316. That is the number you started with, so the answer is right.

items.q: Which calculation checks 70,004 − 36,518 = 33,486?
items.e: Addition is the inverse of subtraction. Add the answer to the number you took away: 33,486 + 36,518 = 70,004. That is the number you started with, so the answer is right.

items.q: Which calculation checks 47,586 + 38,749 = 86,335?

items.q: A theme park had 452,600 visitors in the summer. In the winter it had 186,750 fewer visitors. How many visitors did it have in the summer and winter altogether?

items.q: A shop had £42,350 in its bank account. It paid £18,965 for new stock, then took £27,480 in sales. How much money is in the account now?

items.q: Isla’s mum is a lorry driver. This year she plans to drive 100,000 km. She drove 45,120 km from January to June and 37,465 km from July to October. How many kilometres are left to drive this year?
items.e: Step 1, kilometres driven: 45,120 km + 37,465 km = 82,585 km. Step 2, kilometres left: 100,000 km − 82,585 km = 17,415 km. Check: 17,415 km + 82,585 km = 100,000 km.

items.q: A website had 286,450 visitors in January and 315,780 visitors in February. Another website had 650,000 visitors in the same two months. How many more visitors did the other website have?

items.q: On Saturday, 34,568 fans watched a match at one stadium and 28,795 fans watched a match at another. On Sunday, 72,000 fans watched the cup final. How many more fans watched the cup final than the two Saturday matches?
